new_statements.quote: As common in Bantu, Cuwabo has a binary tone system, intertwining high (H) and toneless (Ø) pitches. [...] The tone-bearing unit in Cuwabo is the mora [p. 86]. Finally, unlike many eastern Bantu languages such as Chewa, Swahili, Mwani (Devos 2008), Makonde (Manus 2003, Kraal 2005), Cuwabo is not subject to penultimate lengthening at the end of a prosodic unit (although the falling H may be viewed as reminiscent of a system formerly marked by penultimate lengthening, as already stated above). [p. 88]
new_statements.citation: Guérois, Rozenn. 2015. A grammar of Cuwabo (Mozambique, Bantu P34). PhD thesis, Université Lumière Lyon 2.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Re-extracted (666 pp., book page = PDF page - 18) with extracted text. p. 104 (book p. 86, §3.1 Generalities) reads verbatim: "As common in Bantu, Cuwabo has a binary tone system, intertwining high (H) and toneless (Ø) pitches.. The tone-bearing unit in Cuwabo is the mora, which represents the smallest phonological unit in a syllabic nucleus (Hayes 1989, Hyman 1992)." Same page: "The emergence of such a contour tone is usually found in a system marked by penultimate lengthening, which is not the case in Cuwabo." p. 106 (book p. 88, end of §3.1) reads verbatim: "Finally, unlike many eastern Bantu languages such as Chewa, Swahili, Mwani (Devos 2008), Makonde (Manus 2003, Kraal 2005), Cuwabo i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Cuwabo (of which Maindo/Mayindo is a dialect) is a lexical- and grammatical-tone language (H vs toneless, mora-counting); the grammar never uses the word 'stress' and explicitly denies the penultimate lengthening that marks phrase-final prominence in neighbouring Bantu languages. No word-stress rule is given; the only word-level regularity noted is that toneless nouns receive a predictable H on the second mora (pp. 98-99) and a doubled H on the penult of a prosodic unit surfaces as falling (p. 86).
new_statements.exceptions: Guérois p. 22 rejects the 1989 NELIMO orthography report's claim that 'todas as vogais sofrem um alongamento, geralmente na penúltima sílaba' (1989: 50) as 'not attested synchronically'; p. 88 allows that the falling H on a phrase-penult mora may be a relic of former penultimate lengthening.
new_statements.domain_note: Prosodic unit / phrase-final position for the lengthening and falling-H statements; lexical tone at word level. Statement is about central Cuwabo (Quelimane), not Maindo: Guérois elicited Mayindo data but did not analyse it (p. 8), and notes Mayindo has 'more Sena-like features' (Sena being toneless, p. 564), so Maindo prosody is unverified.
new_statements.identity_note: Maindo (cwb, main1272) = 'Mayindo' of Guérois 2015, a dialect of Cuwabo/Chuwabu (chuw1238, ISO chw) spoken at Chinde in the Zambezi delta; Maho 2009 files it under P34 'Echuwabo chw.. incl. Maindo cwb' and Wikipedia calls it 'close enough to be a dialect of Chuwabo'. The quoted description is of central Cuwabo (Quelimane), not Maindo; Guérois elicited Mayindo data but did not analyse it and says no dialectological study exists. Maindo is reported to have 'more Sena-like features' (Sena is toneless), so its prosody may differ. Recommend treating main1272 as a variant of chuw1238 rather than a separate catalog entry.

sources.quote: As common in Bantu, Cuwabo has a binary tone system, intertwining high (H) and toneless (Ø) pitches. [...] The tone-bearing unit in Cuwabo is the mora [p. 86]. Finally, unlike many eastern Bantu languages such as Chewa, Swahili, Mwani (Devos 2008), Makonde (Manus 2003, Kraal 2005), Cuwabo is not subject to penultimate lengthening at the end of a prosodic unit (although the falling H may be viewed as reminiscent of a system formerly marked by penultimate lengthening, as already stated above). sources.note: Describes central Cuwabo of Quelimane; §1.3.1 (pp. 7-8) lists Mayindo (Chinde, Zambezi delta, 'more Sena-like features') as one of five Ethnologue dialects, elicited but not analysed. The word 'stress' never occurs; ch. 3 Tones (pp. 85-142): binary H/Ø tone system, TBU = mora, lexical + grammatical tone; p. 88: 'Cuwabo is not subject to penultimate lengthening at the end of a prosodic unit'; p. 22: penult lengthening claimed by the 1989 NELIMO report is 'not attested synchronically'.
